paragraphs: A count-min sketch tracks how often items appear in a stream while using little time and memory. Its usual output is a single estimated count. This paper gives the same data structure a Bayesian interpretation, producing a probability distribution over possible true counts. That distribution describes uncertainty introduced by the hash-based approximation, making the sketch informative beyond its point estimate.

The authors model arriving tokens using a Dirichlet process, which permits an unbounded number of distinct tokens. Properties of this model make it possible to calculate posterior distributions for individual counts. The most probable counts under these distributions reproduce the standard count-min sketch estimates and inherit their probabilistic guarantees.

The paper investigates these estimators using simulated data whose true counts are known. It also considers streams of documents containing collections of tokens. For that setting, a stable beta process provides a model that allows power-law growth in the number of distinct tokens.
neurips-2018-a-bayesian-nonparametric-vi.tldr: A Bayesian interpretation of count-min sketches adds uncertainty estimates while recovering the familiar count estimator.

paragraphs: This paper examines a proposed way to enhance Bloom filters with machine learning. The learned component acts as a preliminary filter by modeling the dataset that the structure represents. The central question is how to reason about the combined structure: adding a learned function creates new design choices, and its contribution needs to be assessed together with the filter itself.

The authors develop a model that clarifies which guarantees can be attached to a learned Bloom filter and which cannot. They also show how to estimate the size the learned function must achieve for the combined design to improve performance. This makes the learning component's size an explicit part of evaluating whether the approach is worthwhile.

The paper then introduces sandwiching as a simple optimization method for learned Bloom filters. It also extends its modeling approach to propose and analyze a learned Bloomier filter. Together, these contributions provide a framework for evaluating and organizing learned filtering structures, rather than assuming that adding learning automatically improves them.
neurips-2018-a-model-for-learned-bloom-f.tldr: The paper models learned Bloom filters, clarifies their guarantees and size requirements, and proposes sandwiching to optimize them.

paragraphs: Online learning in a changing environment requires comparison with decisions that can also change over time. This paper studies dynamic regret, which measures accumulated loss relative to a sequence of comparison decisions. The sequence's path length measures its total movement. The authors establish a lower bound showing that an existing online gradient descent guarantee has a substantial gap in its dependence on this movement.

Their method, Ader, combines multiple experts through an expert-tracking algorithm. Each expert is suited to a particular path length, and combining them lets the method adapt to different amounts of change. Ader achieves regret of order sqrt(T(1 + P_T)), matching the established lower bound in its dependence on the number of rounds and path length.

An improved version uses a surrogate loss to reduce gradient evaluations per round from order log T to one. The authors also extend Ader to use available dynamical models describing the comparison decisions. The contributions therefore address both the theoretical cost of environmental change and the computation needed to adapt.
neurips-2018-adaptive-online-learning-in.tldr: Ader combines experts to achieve optimal dynamic regret and can be implemented with one gradient evaluation per round.

paragraphs: A recurrent dynamics model predicts how a sequence evolves. This paper asks whether the model must always predict at a fixed sampling rate. Its starting observation is that the exact timing of events does not matter for the underlying objective in many sequential prediction tasks. When that is true, the model has room to choose which temporal transitions to predict.

The proposed method, Adaptive Skip Intervals, lets the model select its own prediction intervals. The motivation is that some intervals connect states through transitions that are especially easy to predict. Choosing the interval therefore changes the prediction problem itself, allowing the model to work at a temporal resolution suited to the task.

The authors show that there are prediction tasks where this freedom improves both computational efficiency and prediction accuracy. The finding is conditional on the task: it establishes the usefulness of adaptive timing in suitable settings. Its significance is that temporal abstraction can help a model make better predictions while also reducing the computation those predictions require.
neurips-2018-adaptive-skip-intervals-tem.tldr: Adaptive Skip Intervals lets recurrent models choose prediction timing, improving efficiency and accuracy on suitable tasks.

paragraphs: Graphs such as social networks can help estimate users' missing ratings, but empirical improvements leave a theoretical question unanswered: how many rating observations does a useful graph actually save? This paper studies that question for binary ratings. It focuses on recovering a rating matrix using both observed entries and a related graph.

Under a simple model connecting the graph and rating matrix, the authors characterize a sharp threshold for the number of observed entries needed for recovery. The threshold depends on the quality of the graph information. This turns the graph's value into a sample-complexity statement, describing how much direct rating evidence is needed when the additional structure is available.

The authors also propose a computationally efficient algorithm that reaches this theoretical limit. Experiments show that the algorithm performs well with real-world graphs, extending its empirical appeal beyond the model used for analysis. The recovery threshold remains a result within the stated correlation model, while the experiments provide separate evidence of practical usefulness.
neurips-2018-binary-rating-estimation-wi.tldr: The paper quantifies how graph information reduces the ratings needed for recovery and gives an efficient algorithm attaining that limit.

paragraphs: Many machine learning systems depend on numerical optimization, and optimization methods often need derivatives. This paper focuses on expressions involving matrices and tensors, especially when derivatives must themselves be differentiated. The authors identify a gap in existing frameworks: they do not directly support higher-order matrix and tensor derivatives in the way the proposed framework does.

The contribution is an algorithmic framework that handles matrix and tensor differentiation and extends naturally to higher derivative orders. It supports symbolic differentiation as well as forward and reverse modes of automatic differentiation. This breadth matters because the same approach can serve multiple ways of constructing and evaluating derivatives, rather than being confined to one differentiation mode.

Experiments report higher-order derivative evaluation speedups of one to four orders of magnitude over the compared state-of-the-art frameworks. These are measured computational improvements in the evaluated settings. The paper's stated result concerns the efficiency and capability of derivative computation, a component that optimization systems repeatedly rely on.
neurips-2018-computing-higher-order-deri.tldr: A unified framework computes higher-order matrix and tensor derivatives, with substantial evaluation speedups in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops a convolutional neural network for image deblurring that handles different blur kernels and saturated pixels within one framework. Its design draws on the mathematical structure of image degradation. In particular, the authors use the low-rank properties of pseudo-inverse kernels to guide how the network's convolutional parameters are initialized.

The method first computes generalized low-rank approximations for many blur kernels. It then uses separable filters derived from this process to initialize the network. The authors' analysis finds that the resulting decomposed matrices retain the essential information in an input kernel. This provides the stated basis for handling varied blurs through a unified network.

Experiments on benchmark datasets containing noise and saturated pixels show favorable performance against the compared state-of-the-art methods. The contribution connects a structured approximation of blur kernels with a deep network's image-restoration task. Its reported value is both the ability to accommodate multiple degradation conditions and the quality of the resulting deblurred images.
neurips-2018-deep-non-blind-deconvolutio.tldr: Low-rank approximations of blur kernels guide a deblurring network that handles varied blurs, noise, and saturated pixels.

paragraphs: Autoregressive generation feeds earlier outputs back into the process that produces later ones. This paper challenges the view that such feedback is necessary for successful unconditional generation with stochastic sequence models. The authors argue that feedback can introduce systematic training biases and obscure a useful separation between global information and local variation.

They construct a non-autoregressive deep state space model from an independent noise source and a deterministic transition function. The model explicitly separates global and local uncertainty. This organization supports the paper's view of generation as committing to broader information while allowing local nuances to be forgotten, and contributes to the model's stated interpretability.

Training uses advances in flow-based variational inference to optimize an evidence lower bound. The authors report doing so without annealing, auxiliary losses, or similar interventions. On word generation, the resulting model performs on par with comparable autoregressive models. That result supports the feasibility of their alternative construction for the evaluated task, rather than establishing that autoregressive feedback is unnecessary in every generation setting.
neurips-2018-deep-state-space-models-for.tldr: A non-autoregressive state space model separates global and local uncertainty and matches comparable autoregressive models on word generation.

paragraphs: This paper studies online convex optimization when losses arrive either in an arbitrary sequence or as independent, identically distributed observations. The goal is to obtain efficient algorithms whose excess-risk guarantees reflect sparsity instead of the full number of parameters. This distinction matters when the objective's relevant structure is sparse despite a large parameter space.

For arbitrary loss sequences, the authors develop BOA+. With strongly convex losses, it has several bounds offering different trade-offs between sparsity and convergence rate. Additional convexity assumptions enable rates faster than the usual inverse-square-root dependence on the number of rounds. The faster guarantees are therefore tied to properties of the losses.

For independent, identically distributed losses, the analysis uses a Łojasiewicz assumption. The resulting sparse bounds adapt to the risk's convexity, ranging from a 1/sqrt(T) rate for general convex risk to 1/T for strongly convex risk. The contribution broadens sparse online learning guarantees while showing how stronger curvature can translate into faster learning.
neurips-2018-efficient-online-algorithms.tldr: Efficient online algorithms obtain sparsity-sensitive risk bounds, with faster rates under additional convexity assumptions.

paragraphs: When a pool of human experts makes consequential decisions, the assignment of cases to experts can influence the overall outcome. This paper asks whether optimizing that assignment can improve both accuracy and fairness. Its starting point is that experts may differ in experience, implicit biases, or probabilistic reasoning, while cases are often assigned uniformly at random.

The authors formulate assignment as a sequential decision problem. For different fairness definitions, they reduce it to a sequence of weighted bipartite matching problems, with constraints where needed. Efficient algorithms with approximation guarantees solve these assignments. The method therefore makes fairness and accuracy part of the allocation process.

Posterior sampling helps balance using assignments currently expected to produce good decisions against assignments that teach the system more about experts' preferences and biases. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show significant improvements in both accuracy and fairness. The stated findings suggest that better coordination of existing experts can improve a decision process, even when the intervention acts on assignment rather than directly changing each expert.
neurips-2018-enhancing-the-accuracy-and-.tldr: Learning how to assign decisions to human experts can improve the overall accuracy and fairness of their decisions.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why training neural networks with large batches can reduce accuracy. It studies the loss landscape through the Hessian, which describes local curvature, and through robust optimization. The authors compute the Hessian spectrum without approximation by backpropagating second derivatives, allowing them to examine how training batch size relates to the geometry of the resulting solutions.

Across experiments with multiple networks, the findings do not support saddle points as the cause of the large-batch generalization gap. Instead, large-batch training consistently reaches points with higher Hessian spectra. The authors also connect these points to poorer robustness against adversarial perturbations and show that robust training can favor flatter regions.

The paper further provides theoretical and empirical support that the inner optimization problem in robust training is free of saddle points almost everywhere. Its experiments cover five network architectures, including a residual network, on MNIST and CIFAR-10/100. Together, the results connect batch size, curvature, and adversarial robustness while preserving the distinction between measured training behavior and the stated theoretical result.
neurips-2018-hessian-based-analysis-of-l.tldr: Hessian analysis links large-batch training to higher-curvature solutions and connects flatter regions with adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: A model can be accurate while remaining difficult for people to understand. Methods that optimize interpretability often use convenient substitutes, such as how sparse a model is or how many operations it requires. This paper instead includes human evaluations directly in the optimization process, so the search for an interpretable model is informed by people's responses.

The authors develop an algorithm that seeks predictive and interpretable models while minimizing the number of user studies needed. The number of studies is an explicit concern because human participation is part of evaluating candidate models. The method is demonstrated on several datasets, bringing human judgments into the search rather than relying exclusively on a predefined numerical proxy.

The human-subject results show trends toward different interpretability proxies on different datasets. These trends suggest that the properties people prefer may depend on the task. The finding supports evaluating interpretability in context; it does not establish that any single proxy is always best or that all simple proxies should be discarded.
neurips-2018-human-in-the-loop-interpret.tldr: Human evaluations guide the search for interpretable models, with results suggesting that preferred interpretability proxies vary across tasks.

paragraphs: This paper examines how network architecture influences the linear predictor reached by gradient descent. Its comparison involves full-width linear convolutional networks and linear fully connected networks. Although both settings produce linear predictors, the stated results show that the training process selects solutions with different mathematical characterizations. The architecture therefore matters even in this linear setting.

For a convolutional network of depth L, the limiting predictor is related to an ℓ_(2/L) bridge penalty in the frequency domain. The dependence on L is central: changing depth changes the exponent in the penalty associated with the learned predictor. The result describes a relationship between optimization, depth, and the frequency-domain form of the solution.

For linear fully connected networks, gradient descent instead converges to the hard-margin linear support vector machine solution, regardless of depth. This comparison gives a precise example of implicit bias: the structure used to represent a predictor affects the solution training reaches. The stated convolutional result concerns full-width linear networks, and its characterization is a relation to the bridge penalty.
neurips-2018-implicit-bias-of-gradient-d.tldr: Gradient descent has a depth-dependent frequency-domain bias in full-width linear convolutional networks, unlike linear fully connected networks.

paragraphs: In multi-agent learning, agents may lose some of the feedback they need to update their decisions. This paper studies whether learning can still reach equilibrium under such losses. It focuses on variationally stable games and proposes reweighted online gradient descent, a modification of the classical online gradient descent algorithm.

The authors prove that if every agent uses the proposed method in this class of games, learning converges almost surely to the set of Nash equilibria. Feedback losses may occur asynchronously and may be arbitrarily correlated across agents. The result therefore accommodates irregular and interdependent missing feedback within the stated game setting.

The framework is extended to situations where feedback-loss probabilities are unknown, using estimates constructed from past observations. Another extension combines asynchronous loss with stochastic rewards and still establishes convergence to the equilibrium set. These results broaden the feedback conditions under which multi-agent learning has a convergence guarantee, while retaining variational stability and adoption of the proposed learning rule as key parts of the setting.
neurips-2018-learning-in-games-with-loss.tldr: Reweighted online gradient descent converges to Nash equilibria in variationally stable games despite asynchronous and correlated feedback loss.

paragraphs: Visual question answering combines many different tasks because different questions require different kinds of reasoning about images. Specialized models are appealing, but training specialists does not straightforwardly outperform an independently trained ensemble. This paper proposes a way to develop specialized expertise while preserving the general knowledge models had before specialization.

The method combines multiple choice learning with knowledge distillation. Training examples are dynamically assigned to a subset of models. Assigned models learn to predict the correct answers, while models not assigned those examples learn to imitate their own earlier base models. This gives the unassigned models a learning signal that preserves prior knowledge.

The approach alleviates data deficiency in existing multiple choice learning frameworks, where specialization can leave individual models with too little training data. It is model-agnostic and is also applied to image classification with many labels and few examples per class. Experiments show improvements over the compared baselines in both visual question answering and image classification, supporting the combination of specialization with continued retention of general knowledge.
neurips-2018-learning-to-specialize-with.tldr: Knowledge distillation helps models specialize through dynamic example assignment while retaining their earlier general knowledge.

paragraphs: Fine-grained visual classification distinguishes classes with small visual differences, and collecting labels often requires expert annotators. This paper uses that similarity between classes to motivate maximum-entropy learning. It introduces a training routine for convolutional neural networks that maximizes the entropy of the output probability distribution in fine-grained classification tasks.

Higher output entropy means that the predicted probability distribution is less concentrated. The proposed routine makes this property part of training, connecting the treatment of prediction probabilities to the visual similarity of the categories. The authors provide both theoretical and empirical justification for the approach, rather than presenting the training change solely as an experimental adjustment.

The reported results reach state-of-the-art performance across a variety of fine-grained classification tasks. The method is also reported to be robust across changes in hyperparameters, training-data quantity, and training-label noise. The authors suggest that it could extend to other fine-tuning tasks; that broader extension is presented as a possibility, while the stated performance evidence concerns the evaluated classification tasks.
neurips-2018-maximum-entropy-fine-graine.tldr: Maximum-entropy training improves fine-grained visual classification and shows robustness to training-data, label-noise, and hyperparameter changes.

paragraphs: Sequence generators commonly produce outputs from left to right, giving early choices a strong influence on everything that follows. This paper suggests that this ordering may contribute to limited diversity and difficulty controlling generation. It proposes a decoder that starts with a middle word and expands the sequence in both directions simultaneously.

To coordinate the two growing parts, the architecture includes a dual self-attention mechanism. This mechanism supports information flow and models dependencies among outputs, helping the bidirectional generation process remain consistent. The initial middle word also provides a point around which the output is constructed, making the generation order central to the proposed approach.

The authors evaluate the decoder on synthetic sequence denoising and video captioning. They report significant denoising improvements, competitive captioning performance, and measurable gains in caption diversity. Qualitative analysis also demonstrates control over generation. These findings support the usefulness of middle-out decoding in the evaluated settings, while the claim that left-to-right ordering is a fundamental shortcoming remains the paper's motivating hypothesis.
neurips-2018-middle-out-decoding-ca4f11b.tldr: A decoder that expands from a middle word improves denoising and caption diversity while enabling qualitative control over generation.

paragraphs: Neural networks can manipulate numbers yet struggle when tested on values outside the range seen during training. This paper addresses that numerical extrapolation problem by building arithmetic structure into a neural module. The aim is to encourage operations that continue to make sense when the magnitude of the input changes.

The neural arithmetic logic unit, or NALU, represents numerical quantities through linear activations and manipulates them with primitive arithmetic operators. Learned gates control these operations. The design takes inspiration from arithmetic logic units in traditional processors, while allowing the choice of operations to be learned within a neural network.

Experiments cover tracking time, computing with images of numbers, translating numerical language into scalar values, executing computer code, and counting objects in images. NALU-enhanced networks show substantially better generalization than conventional architectures both within and beyond the training range. They often extrapolate across orders of magnitude beyond trained values. These findings provide empirical support for arithmetic structure as a way to improve numerical generalization.
neurips-2018-neural-arithmetic-logic-uni.tldr: Neural arithmetic logic units use learned arithmetic operations to improve numerical generalization, often far beyond training ranges.

paragraphs: Survival analysis with competing risks models when an event occurs and which of several event types occurs. This paper introduces Lomax delegate racing to represent that competition explicitly. It also aims to make the influence of covariates interpretable in terms of accelerating or delaying the time to an event.

The model represents competition through a potentially infinite collection of sub-risks. This construction can explain non-monotonic covariate effects and relaxes the proportional-hazards assumption, which may be too restrictive. It can also accommodate censoring, missing event times, and missing event types. These capabilities let the same framework represent flexible effects and multiple forms of incomplete outcome information.

The authors provide two inference approaches: a data-augmented Gibbs sampler for moderately sized datasets and stochastic gradient descent for maximum a posteriori inference in large-data applications. Experiments use synthetic and real datasets and report strong performance against competing-risks survival benchmarks. The contribution combines a flexible account of event competition with interpretation and inference methods aimed at different data scales.
neurips-2018-nonparametric-bayesian-loma.tldr: Lomax delegate racing models competing event risks with flexible covariate effects and support for censored or missing outcomes.

paragraphs: Very large observations may be crucial to a classification problem while contributing little to average training error because they are rare. This paper argues that ordinary empirical risk minimization can consequently perform poorly in extreme regions. It develops a classification framework whose objective specifically accounts for prediction quality in those regions.

Under nonparametric heavy-tail assumptions on the class distributions, the authors define an asymptotic notion of risk for extreme observations. They then construct a non-asymptotic approximation and an empirical version based on a fraction of the largest observations. Learning with that objective directs attention toward the part of the input space that an overall error measure can underweight.

The theoretical analysis uses maximal deviation inequalities in low-probability regions to establish good generalization capacity for the resulting classifiers. Numerical experiments illustrate the approach's relevance. The key contribution is a dedicated learning objective and supporting theory for classification in the extremes, with the guarantees grounded in the stated heavy-tail assumptions.
neurips-2018-on-binary-classification-in.tldr: A tail-focused classification objective provides generalization guarantees for extreme observations under heavy-tail assumptions.

paragraphs: Many prediction systems involve both an automated model and another decision-maker. This paper studies a two-stage system in which the model can make a decision or pass it downstream. The central issue is how to choose between those actions when the external decision-maker may have biases or behave inconsistently.

The authors extend rejection learning into learning to defer by accounting for the effects of the other agent. Their algorithm considers potential biases in the external decision-maker as part of learning. This shifts attention toward the performance of the combined decision process: passing a case changes who handles it, so the consequences depend on that person's behavior.

Experiments show that learning to defer can improve accuracy and reduce bias at the system level. Improvements in accuracy, fairness, or both are reported even with inconsistent or biased users. These findings support learning how the two stages should interact, while retaining the qualification that the reported gains need not improve both criteria simultaneously in every setting.
neurips-2018-predict-responsibly-improvi.tldr: Learning when to defer decisions, while accounting for downstream decision-makers, can improve system accuracy and fairness.

paragraphs: Submodular objectives capture diminishing returns in tasks involving diversity or coverage. This paper moves beyond finding a single approximate optimum to representing uncertainty around constrained choices. It defines probabilistic models with log-submodular dependencies of arbitrary order, while requiring valid configurations to belong to the bases of a matroid.

The authors design variational inference algorithms that exploit both the probabilistic model and its combinatorial structure. Their approach minimizes a convex upper bound on the log-partition function, a quantity involved in normalizing the model's probabilities. Greedy algorithms can evaluate the bound efficiently, and first-order optimization methods can optimize it. This makes inference tractable despite a potentially exponential number of valid states.

For facility location and weighted coverage functions, the paper proves an efficiently certifiable e/(e-1) approximation guarantee for the log-partition function. That constant-factor result applies to these specified cases. Experiments on several instances demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, combining practical evidence with guarantees for uncertainty-aware modeling under hard combinatorial constraints.
neurips-2018-provable-variational-infere.tldr: Tractable variational inference quantifies uncertainty in constrained log-submodular models, with constant-factor guarantees for specified objectives.

paragraphs: Stein discrepancies measure how well a sample matches a target distribution and can support sampler selection or goodness-of-fit testing. Existing convergence-determining versions have strong guarantees but require computation that grows quadratically with sample size. Faster testing methods can lose statistical power. This paper seeks a better balance between computational cost and assessment quality.

The authors introduce feature Stein discrepancies, a family of measures that can be approximated cheaply through importance sampling. They show how to construct members of this family that provably determine convergence to a target distribution. They then develop high-accuracy randomized approximations that can be computed in near-linear time.

Experiments evaluate these random feature measures for selecting samplers in approximate posterior inference and for goodness-of-fit testing. They perform as well as or better than quadratic-time kernel Stein discrepancies while taking orders of magnitude less computation. The contribution pairs theoretical convergence-detection properties with empirical evidence that substantial speed gains can preserve useful sample-quality assessments in the tested applications.
neurips-2018-random-feature-stein-discre.tldr: Random feature Stein discrepancies provide near-linear-time sample-quality assessments with strong theory and favorable empirical performance.

paragraphs: An adaptive linear quadratic regulator must control an unknown linear system while incurring quadratic costs. Learning the system and controlling it are intertwined: actions affect immediate costs and the information available for future decisions. This paper combines advances in linear-system estimation with robust controller synthesis to address that joint problem.

The authors present what they identify as the first provably polynomial-time algorithm achieving sublinear regret for this problem. Sublinear regret means that accumulated excess cost grows more slowly than the time horizon. They also prove a lower bound on expected regret in terms of an algorithm's exploration schedule, making the connection between information gathering and control performance explicit.

A numerical study compares the robust adaptive method with other approaches from the adaptive LQR literature. The authors additionally extend it to a demand-forecasting problem with state constraints, demonstrating flexibility beyond the initial formulation. The main contribution is the combination of computational efficiency and a regret guarantee, accompanied by an analysis of the cost of exploration.
neurips-2018-regret-bounds-for-robust-ad.tldr: A robust adaptive LQR algorithm achieves sublinear regret in polynomial time and exposes how exploration affects achievable regret.

paragraphs: Gradient estimation is central to learning in stochastic systems. This paper develops a visual framework for constructing gradient estimators on graphical models using the total derivative rule. Its motivation is that this rule has received less attention than backpropagation and the chain rule, despite offering a useful way to organize derivative calculations.

Within the framework, earlier policy gradient theorems can be derived straightforwardly. The authors also obtain new estimators based on density estimation and a likelihood-ratio gradient that jumps to an intermediate node rather than directly to the objective. These constructions show how considering intermediate parts of a graphical model can lead to alternative gradient estimators.

The methods are evaluated in model-based policy gradient algorithms and achieve good performance. The paper also presents evidence toward explaining the success of PILCO. That explanatory claim remains qualified: the findings help illuminate its behavior. The broader contribution is a common visual framework that both recovers existing gradient results and supports the design of new ones.
neurips-2018-total-stochastic-gradient-a.tldr: The total derivative rule yields a visual framework for deriving existing and new stochastic gradient estimators.
